meta.title: Who really said "There is a land of the living and a land of the dead, and the bridge is love, the only survival, the only meaning"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuine Wilder — the last sentence of The Bridge of San Luis Rey (1927), verified in two scanned 1927 printings.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There is a land of the living and a land of the dead, and the bridge is love, the only survival, the only meaning'?
meta.ogDescription: Real, and it closes the novel. Two 1927 printings print no comma after “dead.” Now US public domain.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This one is real, and it is the last thing the novel says. The Abbess Madre Maria del Pilar thinks it at the close of Part Five, “Perhaps an Intention,” while she is comforting two bereaved women. Two separately scanned 1927 printings carry the passage word for word — and both run “a land of the dead and the bridge is love” straight through, without the comma the popular version adds.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Bridge of San Luis Rey
Part Five, “Perhaps an Intention” — the novel’s closing sentence
the Abbess Madre Maria del Pilar — in thought, not aloud

source.excerpt: “Even now,” she thought, “almost no one remembers Esteban and Pepita, but myself. Camila alone remembers her Uncle Pio and her son; this woman, her mother. But soon we shall die and all memory of those five will have left the earth, and we ourselves shall be loved for a while and forgotten. But the love will have been enough; all those impulses of love return to the love that made them. Even memory is not necessary for love. There is a land of the living and a land of the dead and the bridge is love, the only survival, the only meaning.”
trail: 1927 — the sentence closes the first edition. The Albert & Charles Boni hardcover scanned by the Internet Archive ↗ carries the notice “Copyright, 1927, by Albert & Charles Boni, inc.” and prints the passage exactly as quoted above.
A second printing, same words — the Charles Boni Paper Books edition ↗ reproduces it identically, which is what lets us say the missing comma is the book’s and not one scanner’s slip.
Wikiquote files the line under The Bridge of San Luis Rey (1927) ↗, also without the comma.
2001 — Wikipedia’s article on the novel records that Tony Blair quoted Wilder’s text ↗ at the memorial service for victims of the September 11 attacks.
source.cutTag: The Bridge of San Luis Rey, Part Five (1927)
source.excerptNote: Two things the popular version loses. It is a thought, not a speech — the Abbess is talking to two grieving women while this runs on underneath. And the punctuation: both 1927 printings set “a land of the dead and the bridge is love” with no comma between the clauses.

author.name: Thornton Wilder
author.heading: Who wrote it
author.metaLine: 1897–1975 · American novelist & playwright · three Pulitzer Prizes
author.bio: Thornton Wilder was born in Madison, Wisconsin, in 1897 and won three Pulitzer Prizes — for this novel in 1928, then for the plays Our Town (1938) and The Skin of Our Teeth (1943). The Bridge of San Luis Rey was his second novel: five strangers die when a Peruvian rope bridge collapses, and a friar spends six years trying to prove it was not an accident. Wilder gives the last word not to the friar’s evidence but to an abbess.

copyAttribution: “There is a land of the living and a land of the dead and the bridge is love, the only survival, the only meaning.” — Thornton Wilder, The Bridge of San Luis Rey (New York: Albert & Charles Boni, 1927), closing sentence of Part Five. The widely circulated form adds a comma after “dead”; the 1927 printings do not.

misattribution.heading: What gets lost in the quoting
misattribution.intro: This one is genuine and the work is named correctly nearly everywhere it appears. Two smaller things go missing on the way to the memorial card.

items.who: “a land of the dead, and the bridge is love”
items.why: Both 1927 printings — the Albert & Charles Boni hardcover ↗ and the Charles Boni Paper Books edition ↗ — run the two halves together with no comma: “a land of the dead and the bridge is love.” Small, but it is the difference between a list and a single breath.

The words belong to the Abbess Madre Maria del Pilar, and she is thinking them while she comforts two women who have just lost their families. The novel has spent five parts failing to prove the deaths meant anything; this is what is left over, not the conclusion of an argument.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence as printed, and as the novel ends: “Even memory is not necessary for love. There is a land of the living and a land of the dead and the bridge is love, the only survival, the only meaning.” — The Bridge of San Luis Rey (1927) ↗

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The novel opens on “Friday noon, July the twentieth, 1714,” when the finest bridge in Peru breaks and drops five travellers into the gorge. A Franciscan, Brother Juniper, sees it happen and decides to prove the accident was part of a plan — six years of interviews, one enormous book, and a verdict of heresy. The book is burned in the square, and Wilder is careful to add: with its author.

So the closing sentence is what is left after the proof fails. Not an argument that the deaths meant something, just the Abbess’s thought that love is the only thing that crosses. It is now a funeral reading: Wikipedia’s article on the novel records that Tony Blair quoted Wilder’s text ↗ at the memorial service for victims of the September 11 attacks in 2001.
detailsBody: Wilder’s second novel won the Pulitzer Prize in 1928 and was the best-selling work of fiction that year. He went on to win two more Pulitzers, for the plays Our Town (1938) and The Skin of Our Teeth (1943).

sourcesVerified.claim: The scanned text of this 1927 Albert & Charles Boni printing ends Part Five with: “There is a land of the living and a land of the dead and the bridge is love, the only survival, the only meaning.” — no comma after “dead”. Its copyright page reads “Copyright, 1927, by ALBERT & CHARLES BONI, inc.”

The scanned text of the Charles Boni Paper Books printing carries the identical closing passage, likewise without a comma after “dead”, and its contents page lists Part Five as “PERHAPS AN INTENTION”.
Wikiquote lists the sentence in bold under the section heading The Bridge of San Luis Rey (1927), in the no-comma wording.

Wikipedia gives the publisher as Albert & Charles Boni, release date 1927, the Pulitzer Prize in 1928 and best-selling fiction of that year, and states that Tony Blair quoted Wilder's text during the memorial service for victims of the September 11 attacks in 2001.

Wikipedia states: “All works (excepting sound recordings) first published or released in the United States before January 1, 1931, have lost their copyright protection 95 years later, effective January 1, 2026.”
Wikipedia gives Thornton Wilder's dates as born April 17, 1897 in Madison, Wisconsin and died December 7, 1975, with Pulitzer Prizes for the Novel (1928), and for Drama in 1938 and 1943.
